newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch money market dealers split on rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Dutch money market dealers split on rate hike.

text.p: Dutch money dealers were divided on Tuesday on whether the Dutch central bank would hike its special advances rate this week, after market participant Rabobank said yesterday that this was highly possible.
The special advances rate has been fixed at 2.50 percent since last August.
"It would give a stir in the market and the central bank might not want this to happen, but there are also reasons why such a move is not at all illogical," said one dealer.
Dealers mentioned the increasing trend toward higher rates for call money and other short-dated money rates and the current weakness of the guilder versus the mark.
The guilder was trading at 112.435 per 100 marks at 1440 GMT on Tuesday versus 112.35 at the close on Monday.
On August 22 last year, the day the Dutch central bank trimmed the special advances rate by 20 basis points to 2.50 percent, the guilder was trading at 112.17 per 100 marks.

"The central bank said recently that it would start watching (the rate) if the guilder was trading at 112.40 or lower," said one dealer, adding he rated an increase in the special advances a fair chance.
Call money rates and other short-dated money market rates have been edging up in the last one to two weeks.
Call money was bid at around 2.94 percent today versus 2.87 a week ago and 2.75 percent just before that.
Also, one-month deposits rose step by step to 2.94 percent.
"Those rates will ease again if the Dutch central bank leaves the special advances rate unchanged on Thursday when it sets a new pact," said one dealer.
